title: Take a Flower Apart: Parent Guide
endLine: Flowers make seeds, and pollen must travel for seeds to grow.

scenes.tts: Where do seeds begin inside a flower? In thirty minutes, you can take one apart at the kitchen table. Your child can see where seeds start and try out how pollen travels.
scenes.caption: Where do seeds begin inside a flower? In thirty minutes, you can take one apart at the kitchen table. Your child can see where seeds start and try out how pollen travels.
scenes.visual: Open on a close top-down schematic of one alstroemeria on white paper. Keep the flower large in frame and put a question mark over its center as the narrator asks where seeds begin. Let the view widen to include the hand lens. Use friendly, high-contrast drawings.
scenes.narration: Where do seeds begin inside a flower? In thirty minutes, you can take one apart at the kitchen table. Your child can see where seeds start and try out how pollen travels.

scenes.visual: The same kitchen table scene holds with gentle ambient motion as the petals sway slightly. Clean dark bold title text fades in over the upper part of the white paper: 'Take a Flower Apart' with a smaller subtitle 'Parent Guide'.

scenes.tts: Here, your child practices looking closely and sorting pieces from the outside in. They also practice making a guess and checking what they see. You peel one flower ring by ring, then play bee with colored sugar.
scenes.caption: Here, your child practices looking closely and sorting pieces from the outside in. They also practice making a guess and checking what they see. You peel one flower ring by ring, then play bee with colored sugar.
scenes.visual: Same top-down tabletop view. The title fades out. On the white paper, faint concentric dotted rings sketch themselves around the flower as the hand lens glides smoothly over the petals. Off to the right on a small tray, three schematic paper cupcake liners slide into view, two holding neat mounds of red and blue sugar crystals.
scenes.narration: Here, your child practices looking closely and sorting pieces from the outside in. They also practice making a guess and checking what they see. You peel one flower ring by ring, then play bee with colored sugar.

scenes.tts: Gather two or three single flowers, like alstroemeria or petunias. If a cat lives in or visits your home, never bring in true lilies or daylilies. Even pollen or vase water can kill them. Add paper, tape, a hand lens and scissors. Gather three liners, two sugar colors and swabs.
scenes.caption: Gather two or three single flowers, like alstroemeria or petunias. If a cat lives in or visits your home, never bring in true lilies or daylilies. Even pollen or vase water can kill them. Add paper, tape, a hand lens and scissors. Gather three liners, two sugar colors and swabs.
scenes.visual: Same tabletop workspace neatly arranged from above. Simple, bold schematic drawings settle in place one by one as named: two single flowers, a clear red-crossed warning badge over a schematic true lily next to a small sitting cat silhouette (stacked labels 'Cat lives here or visits?' and 'No lilies or daylilies'), then white paper, tape roll, hand lens, small scissors, three cupcake liners, red and blue sugar mounds, and cotton swabs. Keep at most six grouped clusters visible at once.
scenes.narration: Gather two or three single flowers, like alstroemeria or petunias. If a cat lives in or visits your home, never bring in true lilies or daylilies. Even pollen or vase water can kill them. Add paper, tape, a hand lens and scissors. Gather three liners, two sugar colors and swabs.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child throughout. Do all cutting and hold any glass lens yourself. Keep swabs, sugar, and small bits away from children under four. Keep them out of mouths, noses, and ears. Call nine one one if choking. Never point the lens at the sun.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child throughout. Do all cutting and hold any glass lens yourself. Keep swabs, sugar, and small bits away from children under four. Keep them out of mouths, noses, and ears. Call nine one one if choking. Never point the lens at the sun.
scenes.visual: Keep the tabletop in view. Show the adult seated with the child and holding the scissors or glass lens. Keep the lens away from a simple sun symbol. Group the swab, sugar, and flower bits beside these two labels: 'Keep away from children under 4' and 'Call 911 if choking'.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child throughout. Do all cutting and hold any glass lens yourself. Keep swabs, sugar, and small bits away from children under four. Keep them out of mouths, noses, and ears. Call nine one one if choking. Never point the lens at the sun.

scenes.tts: Let your child inspect one flower and count its petals. Ask, "What do you think is in the very middle?" Peel the outer sepals, then the petals, taping each ring on paper. Dab the thin stalks inside to spot powdery pollen, then tape them next.
scenes.caption: Let your child inspect one flower and count its petals. Ask, "What do you think is in the very middle?" Peel the outer sepals, then the petals, taping each ring on paper. Dab the thin stalks inside to spot powdery pollen, then tape them next.
scenes.visual: Back to the full bright tabletop and white sheet of paper. The schematic flower sits in the center as the hand lens hovers and pulses gently. As each step is spoken, the outer sepals lift and land cleanly in a taped outer ring ('Sepals'), then the bright petals lift into a second ring inside them ('Petals'), then the thin stalks tap a small dark corner of paper to leave yellow dots ('Pollen') before lining up in a third smaller ring.
scenes.narration: Let your child inspect one flower and count its petals. Ask, "What do you think is in the very middle?" Peel the outer sepals, then the petals, taping each ring on paper. Dab the thin stalks inside to spot powdery pollen, then tape them next.

scenes.tts: Ask, "Where do you think seeds will grow?" Slice across the base of the central part and tape the pieces down. Look for pale beads. Pollen lands on the tip, and the beads inside the base can become seeds.
scenes.caption: Ask, "Where do you think seeds will grow?" Slice across the base of the central part and tape the pieces down. Look for pale beads. Pollen lands on the tip, and the beads inside the base can become seeds.
scenes.visual: On the same paper, show an adult hand slice across the swollen base of the central part and tape the pieces down. Show the pale beads inside the cut base. On a small schematic of the same intact central part, show a pollen grain land on its tip. Keep the tip and the beads visually distinct.
scenes.narration: Ask, "Where do you think seeds will grow?" Slice across the base of the central part and tape the pieces down. Look for pale beads. Pollen lands on the tip, and the beads inside the base can become seeds.

scenes.tts: Use colored sugar as pretend pollen. Check the label for food or dye allergies. Never taste plants or sugar. Do not blow on the sugar. Imagine asking why bees visit flowers. What might your child say, and how would you answer?
scenes.caption: Use colored sugar as pretend pollen. Check the label for food or dye allergies. Never taste plants or sugar. Do not blow on the sugar. Imagine asking why bees visit flowers. What might your child say, and how would you answer?
scenes.visual: The camera pans smoothly across the same wooden table to the tray with three cupcake liners (red sugar, blue sugar, empty) and a schematic cotton swab resting beside a stylized friendly bee drawing. A clean, high-contrast question card opens over the tray reading: 'Why do bees visit flowers?'
scenes.narration: Use colored sugar as pretend pollen. Check the label for food or dye allergies. Never taste plants or sugar. Do not blow on the sugar. Imagine asking why bees visit flowers. What might your child say, and how would you answer?

scenes.visual: The question card 'Why do bees visit flowers?' and smaller sub-prompt 'How would you reply?' remain crisp and steady on screen while the stylized schematic bee hovers slowly in a figure-eight near a drawn flower and a thin calm progress bar fills smoothly over 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Your child might say the bee wants to help the flower. Explain that bees visit for food. They collect nectar and pollen. As a bee visits flowers, pollen sticks to its hairy body and rubs off on the next flower.
scenes.caption: Your child might say the bee wants to help the flower. Explain that bees visit for food. They collect nectar and pollen. As a bee visits flowers, pollen sticks to its hairy body and rubs off on the next flower.
scenes.visual: The question card transforms smoothly into a schematic side view of the stylized bee sipping nectar from one flower. Bright yellow pollen dots cling gently to fuzzy lines on the bee's body as it flies across to a second flower, where several yellow dots drift off onto the center of the second flower. Clear label: 'Bees come for food'.
scenes.narration: Your child might say the bee wants to help the flower. Explain that bees visit for food. They collect nectar and pollen. As a bee visits flowers, pollen sticks to its hairy body and rubs off on the next flower.

scenes.tts: Put the liners on a tray. Add a small spoonful of each color to its own liner. Leave the third empty. Ask, "What will the empty flower look like after the bee visits?" Have your child dab each liner in order with the swab.
scenes.caption: Put the liners on a tray. Add a small spoonful of each color to its own liner. Leave the third empty. Ask, "What will the empty flower look like after the bee visits?" Have your child dab each liner in order with the swab.
scenes.visual: Return to the top-down tray on the wooden table with the three cupcake liners in a row: red sugar on the left, blue sugar in the middle, empty white liner on the right. A schematic cotton swab arcs smoothly into the red liner (picking up red specks), dips into the blue liner (picking up blue specks and dropping red ones), and taps the empty third liner. The hand lens glides over the third liner to magnify bright red and blue specks resting inside.
scenes.narration: Put the liners on a tray. Add a small spoonful of each color to its own liner. Leave the third empty. Ask, "What will the empty flower look like after the bee visits?" Have your child dab each liner in order with the swab.

scenes.tts: Look for both colors in the last liner. Toss the sugar and wash hands together. Ask your child to point to where seeds begin. Petals can attract animals. Stalks make the pollen those animals carry.
scenes.caption: Look for both colors in the last liner. Toss the sugar and wash hands together. Ask your child to point to where seeds begin. Petals can attract animals. Stalks make the pollen those animals carry.
scenes.visual: Begin on the red and blue specks in the last liner. Pull back to the finished sheet as the adult clears the sugar. Show a handwashing icon. Then highlight the petals and pollen stalks in turn.
scenes.narration: Look for both colors in the last liner. Toss the sugar and wash hands together. Ask your child to point to where seeds begin. Petals can attract animals. Stalks make the pollen those animals carry.
